response.consequence: On shutdown or rebalance with a timeout and more than one flusher process, the later processes may be left alive. They are daemon processes, so they die when the parent exits. Until then they can keep flushing, or keep Redis and Kafka producers open, while the strategy is treated as joined.
response.explanation: In the new per-process loop in SpanFlusher.join, when the remaining time reaches zero the code does `break`. That exits the loop before `process.terminate()` runs for the current process and for every process after it. The old single-process code always called terminate() after the wait loop. With several flusher processes, a slow first process can use up the timeout. The later processes are then never terminated and keep running, with `stopped` already set, after join returns.
response.title: join() skips terminating remaining flusher processes once the deadline expires

response.consequence: The test can still fail intermittently if the flusher has not flushed by the time the messages are checked. The added wait gives a false sense of stability.
response.explanation: test_basic patches "time.sleep" to `lambda _: None` at its start. The added `import time` followed by `time.sleep(0.1)` looks up the patched attribute on the time module, so it returns immediately. The comment says it gives the flusher time to process after the drift change, but it waits for nothing. test_flusher.py avoids this because it uses `from time import sleep`, which was bound before the patch and so is the real function. The intended synchronization in test_basic does not happen. The assertion `(msg,) = messages` still depends on step.join() and on flusher timing.
response.title: time.sleep(0.1) added to test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

response.consequence: After a hang, a duplicate flusher runs on the same shards. This can produce duplicate segments in Kafka and leak processes. The leak grows with each restart until MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS is exceeded.
response.explanation: The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. That class derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`). The isinstance check is therefore always False for real processes, and `kill()` is never reached. When a flusher is declared hung (`cause == "hang"`) and is still alive, `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement while the old process keeps running. The old process keeps flushing the same shards, so two flushers now work on the same shard buffer. The same isinstance check in `join()` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either.
response.title: Hung flusher process is never killed because isinstance check excludes SpawnProcess
